summary: An update on NETRJS, the private remote job entry protocol that UCLA's Campus Computing Network published in RFC 189 and provided to the network for over two years. NETRJS gives network access to CCN's RJS software. It was replaced by RFC 740.

eli5.summary: A way to send jobs to a big computer from far away had been running for two years. This note updates how it works. A later paper replaced it.

questions: remote job entry on the arpanet
subtitle: Improvements to the NETRJS remote job entry service after two years of use

tldr.problem: NETRJS, the remote job entry service at UCLA-CCN, had been running for over two years but had reliability issues and poorly defined protocol details.
tldr.mechanism: UCLA rewrote the server software with internal improvements (fixing the 'squish' problem), stricter timeouts, better error messages, and clarified the protocol based on implementation experience.
tldr.outcome: The new version was more robust; by October 1973, it was processing over 1,000 jobs per month across multiple implementations at research sites.

today: RFC 599 is Historic and was replaced by RFC 740. NETRJS served the early ARPANET research community for years, pioneering remote job entry on a network before email and interactive computing became dominant.

sections.title: NETRJS Service Update
sections.content:
NETRJS (the ARPANET interface to UCLA-CCN's RJS, or Remote Job Service) had been available on the network for over two years. RFC 599 reports improvements made when UCLA redeployed the server in September 1973 to coincide with a major OS/360 update.

By this time, NETRJS had implementations at RAND, UCLA-NMC, Illinois, Utah, MIT, Harvard, UCSB, and other sites. In October 1973 alone, the system processed 1,373 batch jobs, totaling 49,400 cards read and 822,900 lines printed.
sections.eli5: A service for sending computing jobs to UCLA's big computer had been working for a while. UCLA rewrote it to be better, and more sites were using it.

sections.title: Key Improvements
sections.content:
The main problems fixed were: the squish problem (where output could be lost if a remote host crashed before receiving data already sent), new timeout rules (3-minute signon timeout, 5-minute data transfer timeout), and better error messages to distinguish problems at CCN, the user site, or in the network. Users could now use Control-C to abort a session.

On the protocol side, NETRJS moved to new socket numbers (71, 73, 75 instead of 11, 13, 15) and clarified character mappings for EBCDIC and ASCII terminals. The RFC also documents three variants: ASCII-63 (for tty-like keyboards), ASCII-68, and EBCDIC.
sections.eli5: UCLA fixed a bug where data could disappear. They added timeouts to prevent hangups. They moved to new socket numbers and wrote down exactly how text should be converted between different character sets.

sections.title: Usage and Status
sections.content:
NETRJS offered five key terminal options: data format (truncated or compressed), automatic job resubmission after a crash, automatic output restart after broken connections, password protection, and suppression of punch separators. Each site could choose which options suited its users.

The RFC warns Tenex users about pitfalls in one commonly available Tenex RJS implementation and lists references for the complete NETRJS specification, remote operator commands, and character mapping details. RFC 599 was itself replaced by RFC 740.
sections.eli5: Different network sites could pick options for how the service worked. There was a warning for users on one type of computer that their version had some quirks.
